story.title: Fluent text can put the right entity in the wrong role
paragraphs: In the paper's Table 2 example, the input gives Round Rock as the largest city of Williamson County and Georgetown as its county seat; the output calls Georgetown the largest city and omits the county seat. The sentence reads naturally, yet it contains a distorted fact and a missing one, each needing a different repair, and a single overlap score cannot say which.

Earlier human evaluations of data-to-text systems covered few samples, datasets, models, or error dimensions. Here annotators locate every error and record its type and severity, giving each model an error profile instead of one number.

mechanism.title: Faithfulness and content selection are distinct requirements
paragraphs: The study adapts the Multidimensional Quality Metrics (MQM) framework, via the PolyTope scheme for summarization, to eight error types. Inaccuracy Intrinsic distorts information in the input; Inaccuracy Extrinsic adds information absent from it; Addition, narrower than hallucination, is unnecessary material taken from the input. Omission, Positive-Negative Aspect, Duplication, Word Form, and Word Order complete the set. Addition versus Omission matters most for ToTTo, where only highlighted cells should be described.

Each error span gets a type and a severity: minor, major, or critical. Five annotators, selected from eight by a qualification test, labeled 1,600 outputs (80 inputs × four datasets × five models), each twice; outputs whose two error scores diverged too much were replaced, and annotators did not know which model produced an output.

evidence.title: An architectural improvement can move errors between categories
paragraphs: Copying preserves input content but also pulls in content the description does not need: on ToTTo, the copy model's Omission score falls by more than half while its Addition score more than doubles (Table 5). The paper attributes the extra additions to an auto-regressive decoder that copies long input spans and is hard to interrupt.

BLEU's overall trend agrees with human evaluation, but the paper reports a Pearson correlation of 0.61 between BLEU and the accuracy score and only 0.08 for fluency (Section 6), and rankings of close models can flip, as on E2E. Pre-training has the largest effect in Table 3: pre-trained models beat the others by a wide margin on every dataset except E2E.

reading_notes: Re-read precise MQM/PolyTope definitions, severity formula (Section 4.3, ratio 1:3:7, omission length 1), annotation protocol and Tables 2–6. Especially important: Addition means irrelevant source content, Extrinsic means unsupported content; do not conflate them. v5 demo uses the Table 2 triples and output verbatim; the paper reports types but not severities for that example.

demo.title: Annotate the output, then compare with the paper
demo.description: The study scores outputs from human error annotations: each error segment receives a type and a severity, the severity weight is multiplied by the segment length, and the total is normalized by the word count (Section 4.3). Annotate the paper’s Table 2 output yourself, then reveal the paper’s annotation.
demo.note: Adapted: input triples and output verbatim from Table 2; error types from Section 4.1; severities and the 1:3:7 ratio from Sections 4.2–4.3; omission length fixed to 1 (footnote 3). Computed: every score, using Equations 1–2 over this single output (20 words, punctuation not counted). The paper normalizes by all annotated outputs of a dataset (80 per model), so one output moves a system score far less. Table 2 does not report severities; its annotation is scored for every severity combination. The measured Table 6 averages appear under Reading the evidence.
